opus-5.5.text:
I think further than a lot of people expect. When people say models "can't learn on the job," they're often underrating how much you can get from two things we already have: a very long context window and very strong in-context learning. If you can put a few hundred thousand or a million tokens of relevant material in front of a model, like the codebase, the past tickets, the style guide, the last month of conversations, a lot of what a human gets from their first few weeks at a job, the model gets in a few minutes. It's not the same mechanism as a human slowly consolidating memories, but functionally it covers a surprising amount of the gap.

Then there's the training side. Pretraining plus RL on a very wide distribution of tasks keeps generalizing better than I'd have predicted. Each time we broaden the environments, the models pick up skills we didn't explicitly train for. So my honest guess is that the current paradigm, scaled up and broadened, gets you to models that can do most of what a very capable remote knowledge worker does, including a lot of what we'd call novel research work.

Where I think continual learning really matters is the long tail: the job where the critical knowledge is tacit, spread over months, never written down, and only absorbed by being there and making mistakes. Today's models are weaker there, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. But I see it as an engineering problem, not a wall. There are several plausible ways to get there: longer context, better memory systems, periodic fine-tuning on a deployment's own data, or something more native. I'd be surprised if it ends up being the thing that stops progress.

So my short answer: the existing paradigm can take us very far, plausibly to the point where these systems are economically transformative, and continual learning is more likely to be the last 10 or 20 percent that gets solved along the way than a fundamental barrier.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pretraining and RL generalizing across tasks, but does not place them between evolution and learning within an individual lifetime.

r002.rationale: It says in-context learning can cover some of the gap from a human’s first weeks at work, but does not identify it as a shorter-lived analogue of on-the-job learning.

r003.rationale: It compares a million-token context of relevant material to what a human learns over the first few weeks at a job, which the model can absorb in minutes.

r004.rationale: The response expects the current paradigm to get very far, but says continual learning may be needed for the last 10–20%; it does not say scaling plus in-context learning suffices to produce the stated outcome without it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it can take us surprisingly far, further than most people expected even a couple of years ago, but I also think continual learning is one of the real remaining gaps, so let me try to separate those two things.

On the first point: the paradigm we have now is pretraining, then a lot of reinforcement learning on top, and then increasingly long-horizon agentic tasks where the model is operating in an environment, using tools, checking its own work. Every time someone has said "this is going to run out," the scaling has mostly kept going. And what's happened with RL in particular is that we've found a way to turn compute into capability on tasks that have some verifiable signal, like code, math, and increasingly things like scientific reasoning and multi-step work. So in domains where you can define what good looks like, I think we're going to keep getting models that are very capable within a single context, with no weight updates at all.

The thing that's interesting is how much of what looks like "learning on the job" you can actually fake with context. Humans learn on the job partly by updating their brains and partly by writing things down, building habits, having systems around them. A model with a long context, with memory tools, with the ability to read documents and take notes to itself, gets a nontrivial fraction of that without touching the weights. And the context windows keep growing and the models keep getting better at using them. So I'd say a lot of economically valuable work, maybe most of it, is reachable before you solve continual learning in the deep sense.

But I don't want to oversell it. There's a real difference between a model that's read everything about your company in context and an employee who has worked there for three years. Some of that is tacit knowledge that never gets written down. Some of it is that the human has made a thousand small corrections and each one changed them a little. We don't have a clean way to do that yet. Fine-tuning is clumsy, it's expensive, it risks damaging other capabilities, and nobody wants to do a gradient update every time a model makes a mistake. So I think of continual learning as one of maybe three or four remaining big ideas, alongside things like reliability over very long horizons and some aspects of taste or judgment.

My honest guess, and I've been wrong on timelines in both directions, is that continual learning is going to be solved partly by the brute approach, meaning the models and their scaffolding just get good enough that it matters less, and partly by some genuine research advance that we don't have yet. I'd put decent odds on something meaningful within a few years. But even if it took longer, I don't think it's the thing standing between us and models that are transformative. The current paradigm, pushed hard, gets you a lot of the way there. It's just that the last part of the way, the part where the model is a colleague that actually grows, probably needs it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pretraining and reinforcement learning, but does not place them between evolution and learning within an individual lifetime.

r002.rationale: It describes learning through context and memory tools as approximating on-the-job learning without changing model weights, including learning within a single context.

r003.rationale: It mentions growing context windows but does not explain the scope of a million-token context or compare it with days or weeks of human reading.

r004.rationale: It says scaling the current pretraining and RL paradigm, with context and scaffolding, could make models transformative and enable most economically valuable work before continual learning is solved.

astra-6.text:
I think it can take us quite far. I’d separate two questions: how capable can a model become during training, and how much does it need to learn from experience once you put it to work? Those are related, but they’re not the same thing.

A model can have fixed weights and still adapt to a task through its context. You can give it a codebase, explain what you want, let it try things, and give it feedback. It’s learning something in a functional sense, even if that information isn’t being incorporated into the weights. So I wouldn’t assume that the absence of continual weight updates puts a hard ceiling on its ability to do useful work.

But there’s a real question about accumulation. If you hire someone, after six months they understand your organization, they know which approaches failed, and they have judgment that they didn’t have on day one. You want an AI system to accumulate that experience too. Putting everything into context might get you some distance, but it may be an awkward or inefficient way to do it.

So my guess is that the existing paradigm can produce very powerful systems, including systems that do a substantial amount of economically valuable work. I’m less certain that it gives you the most efficient way to deploy those systems over long periods. Continual learning could be enormously important without being a prerequisite for reaching a very high level of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes training from experience-based learning but does not characterize pre-training and reinforcement learning as lying between evolution and individual-lifetime learning.

r002.rationale: It says a model can adapt through context and contrasts that with accumulating experience, but does not identify in-context learning as a shorter-lived analogue of human on-the-job learning.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between a million-token context and days or weeks of human reading.

r004.rationale: It says the existing paradigm could produce powerful systems that do substantial economically valuable work, but does not say that scaling pre-training and reinforcement learning with in-context learning could suffice for a “country of geniuses in a data center.”

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can take us quite far, but there are two questions that are worth separating. One is: can a model learn, during training, the general capabilities it needs to do a very wide range of jobs? The other is: once you put it in a particular job, how does it acquire all the context that’s specific to that job?

For the first, I don’t see a clear reason that the current paradigm has to hit a wall before models become extremely capable. You can learn a lot about how to solve unfamiliar problems without having encountered those exact problems in training. That’s what generalization is.

But the second question is a real issue. If you hire a person, they learn how your organization works, they remember mistakes, they build up expertise over months. A model that starts fresh every time is missing something important there.

Now, some of that can be handled without changing the model’s weights. You can put information in the context, give it access to records of its previous work, let it retrieve relevant material. The question is how far those mechanisms get you, and where you actually need learning that changes the model itself.

So I wouldn’t say continual learning is a prerequisite for very powerful AI. I would say it could make a big difference to how useful that AI is over long periods of time. And I’m uncertain about whether it turns out to be a fundamental bottleneck or something we solve with a fairly straightforward extension of what we already do.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes general capabilities learned during training from job-specific context, but does not place pre-training and reinforcement learning between evolution and individual-lifetime learning.

r002.rationale: It says context and records can help with job-specific information, but does not identify in-context learning as a shorter-lived analogue of human on-the-job learning.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss a million-token context or compare its learning scope to days or weeks of human reading.

r004.rationale: It says continual learning may not be required for very powerful AI, but does not propose scaling pre-training, reinforcement learning, and in-context learning together as sufficient for a “country of geniuses in a data center.”
